about: Overview

Conveyancing is the legal work involved in moving the ownership of property, or a mortgage over property, from one person to another. In England and Wales it covers buying and selling homes, remortgaging, adding or removing an owner, and a range of related jobs such as dealing with a lease or a new build contract. The person doing the work is called a conveyancer, and they may be a solicitor or a licensed conveyancer.

For most people, conveyancing is something they only deal with a handful of times in their life. It usually sits alongside some of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make, so it helps to understand the basic shape of the work before it starts. The legal side is not just paperwork. It is about making sure you know what you are buying, that the person selling actually has the right to sell, and that your money and your lender's money are protected.

A good conveyancer acts as a guide as well as a lawyer. They explain what is happening at each stage, tell you what they need from you and when, and warn you early if something could cause a problem. They also deal with the people you do not see, such as the other side's solicitor, the mortgage lender, the local authority, HM Land Registry and HMRC or the Welsh Revenue Authority.

list: Your legal title, so you own what you think you own
Your money, which passes through a regulated client account
Your lender's security, which most mortgage offers depend on
Your rights over things like access, drains and boundaries
Your position if something turns out to be different from what you were told

about: The law of conveyancing is largely the same across England and Wales, but there are differences. The biggest is property tax. In England, buyers may pay Stamp Duty Land Tax to HMRC. In Wales, the equivalent is Land Transaction Tax, collected by the Welsh Revenue Authority. Some renting and leasehold rules also differ. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own separate systems, and the firms we introduce handle property in England and Wales.

A typical sale or purchase involves more people than most clients expect. There is usually an estate agent, a conveyancer for the buyer and one for the seller, at least one mortgage lender and broker, a surveyor, and often other buyers and sellers further along the chain. Your conveyancer only acts for you and, where relevant, your lender. They cannot speak for the other side or make other people in the chain move faster, but they can chase, explain what is holding things up and keep your part of the transaction moving.
Leaflegal is not a law firm and does not give legal advice. We introduce you to one regulated firm that handles your kind of matter, and the firm will look at your own situation.
What we cover
Conveyancing is a broad heading. Different jobs need different checks, and some firms specialise in particular kinds of work. These are the matters we introduce people for.

The buyer's conveyancer checks the title, orders searches, reviews the contract and the seller's answers, reports on anything unusual, and handles the money and registration. You can read more on our page about buying a home.

The seller's conveyancer prepares the contract pack, deals with the buyer's questions, pays off the mortgage and sends the seller the balance. Preparing early is the single biggest thing a seller can do to avoid delay. See our page on selling a home.
Most home movers have a sale and a purchase that need to happen on the same day. One firm can run both and keep them in step.
Switching to a new lender needs the new lender's legal work done, the old mortgage paid off and the new one registered. Some lenders offer this free, while others leave you to instruct a firm.
Adding or removing someone from the ownership of a home without selling it. This often follows a marriage, a separation or a gift within a family, and it usually needs the lender's consent.

We also introduce first time buyers, landlords buying to let, people buying new build homes from developers and people buying leasehold flats. Each of these has its own extra checks, and it is worth telling us about them when you fill in the form so we can match you to a firm that does this work regularly.
Choosing a firm

Most people choose a conveyancer on price alone, or take whoever the estate agent suggests. Price matters, but it is not the only thing worth weighing up. Conveyancing is a service you will be in contact with for weeks or months, and the way a firm works can make a real difference to how stressful the process feels.

Both can do residential conveyancing. Solicitors are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority, and licensed conveyancers by the Council for Licensed Conveyancers. Both must carry professional indemnity insurance and hold client money under strict rules. A solicitor's firm may also be able to help with related matters such as wills or separation, while a licensed conveyancer focuses on property.

If you are using a mortgage, the firm usually has to be on your lender's panel, which is the list of firms the lender trusts to act for it. Most established firms are on the panels of the major lenders, but it is worth checking, particularly with smaller or specialist lenders.

list: Who will handle my file day to day, and how do I reach them?
How do you keep clients updated, and how often?
Is the quote fixed, and what would make it go up?
Do you do much work with this kind of property, such as leasehold or new build?
Are you on my lender's panel?
Do you belong to any quality schemes, such as the Law Society's Conveyancing Quality Scheme?

about: Some firms work mainly online and by phone, with case tracking portals and set processes. Others are local high street practices that know the area and its usual issues. Neither is automatically better. What matters is that the firm is responsive, explains things clearly and has the experience your transaction needs.
Our form asks a few questions about your property and your plans so we can introduce you to a firm that handles that kind of work.
Timescales

How long conveyancing takes is one of the questions people ask most, and one of the hardest to answer. A simple remortgage may take a few weeks. A purchase in a long chain with a leasehold flat at one end can take several months. The legal work itself is only part of the timetable.

list: The length of the chain and how ready everyone in it is
How quickly the seller's paperwork is prepared
How long the local authority takes to return searches
Whether the mortgage offer is issued promptly
Leasehold management packs from landlords and managing agents
Problems found on the title, such as missing rights or unclear boundaries
How quickly each party answers questions and signs documents

about: Most transactions follow a similar order. The firm is instructed and carries out identity and money checks. The title and contract are reviewed and searches are ordered. Enquiries are raised and answered. The buyer's mortgage offer arrives and the buyer is reported to. Contracts are signed and exchanged, and a completion date is fixed. Completion follows, and the change of ownership is registered.

In England and Wales, nobody is legally bound to buy or sell until contracts are exchanged. Until then either side can pull out. Once contracts are exchanged, both sides are committed and the completion date is fixed. The gap between exchange and completion is agreed between the parties and can range from the same day to several weeks.

Completion is not quite the end of the legal work. The buyer's conveyancer still has to submit the tax return and pay any tax due, then apply to HM Land Registry to register the new owner and any new mortgage. For leasehold property, notices are usually sent to the landlord or managing agent. The seller's conveyancer makes sure the old mortgage is formally removed from the register. Most of this happens in the background and does not need anything from you, but registration can take some time to show on the public register.

Your conveyancer can usually give a rough idea of timescales once they have seen the paperwork, but they cannot control everyone in the chain. Starting early and answering questions quickly are the two things most within your control.
Costs
Conveyancing costs come in three main parts. Understanding the difference makes it much easier to compare quotes.

This is what the firm charges for its own work. Many firms quote a fixed fee for straightforward residential work, often linked to the price of the property and whether it is freehold or leasehold. Some add separate charges for extra tasks, such as dealing with a gifted deposit, a Help to Buy loan, a new build or a lease.

These are payments the firm makes to other organisations on your behalf. Examples include search fees, HM Land Registry fees, bank transfer fees, identity check fees and, for leasehold property, fees charged by the landlord or managing agent. A clear quote lists disbursements separately.

Buyers may need to pay Stamp Duty Land Tax in England or Land Transaction Tax in Wales. The amount depends on the price, the type of buyer and whether reliefs or higher rates apply. Rates and thresholds change, so check GOV.UK or the Welsh Revenue Authority, or ask the firm to confirm the figure for you. VAT is also charged on the legal fee and on some disbursements.

A low headline fee can rise quickly if extras are added later. When comparing quotes, look at the total including VAT and disbursements, check what is included, and ask what would happen if the transaction fell through. Some firms offer reduced or no fees if a sale or purchase does not go ahead, so it is worth asking.

It also helps to know when money is needed. Most firms ask for a payment on account at the start to cover searches and early disbursements. Buyers usually need their deposit ready before exchange and the rest of their funds, along with any tax, shortly before completion. Your firm will send a statement showing what is due and when, and it should never ask you to send money to a new bank account by email without confirming it by phone first.
Leaflegal is free to use. The firm we introduce you to pays us for the introduction, and that never changes what you pay them.
Getting ready

A lot of conveyancing delay comes from waiting for information that could have been gathered at the start. A little preparation helps your firm move faster and reduces the chance of last minute surprises.

list: Photo ID, such as a passport or driving licence
Proof of address, such as a recent bank statement or council tax bill
Details of where your money is coming from, with bank statements going back several months
Contact details for your estate agent and mortgage broker, if you have them
Your title deeds, or the name of your mortgage lender
Guarantees and warranties for work done to the property
Building regulation certificates and planning documents for any alterations
Certificates for things like replacement windows, boilers and electrical work
For leasehold property, your lease and your landlord or managing agent's details
Your mortgage in principle or offer
Evidence of your deposit, and gift letters if family are helping
Details of any scheme you are using, such as a Lifetime ISA or shared ownership
Your answers to any questions the firm sends, returned promptly

about: All regulated firms must check where the money in a property transaction comes from. This is a legal requirement under money laundering rules, not a sign that anyone suspects you. Expect to be asked for bank statements and an explanation of any large payments in or out. If a relative is gifting money, they will usually need to prove their identity and where the money came from too.

Once the transaction is under way, the most useful thing you can do is respond quickly. Read what your conveyancer sends, ask if anything is unclear and return signed documents promptly. Tell the firm straight away about any change in your plans, such as a new mortgage product, a change in the amount you are borrowing, someone else joining the purchase or a change in your move date. Small changes can affect paperwork that has already been prepared.
Having these ready when the firm first contacts you can save days or even weeks later in the process.
faqs: The basics
What is conveyancing?

Conveyancing is the legal work involved in transferring the ownership of property, or registering a mortgage against it. It includes checking the title, carrying out searches, preparing or reviewing the contract, handling the money and registering the change at HM Land Registry. It applies to buying, selling, remortgaging and changing who owns a home.
Do I legally have to use a conveyancer?

It is possible to do your own conveyancing in some situations, but it is rare and difficult. If you have a mortgage, your lender will almost always insist that a regulated firm acts for it. Most people use a professional because the legal and financial risks of getting things wrong are high and hard to put right later.
What is the difference between freehold and leasehold?

Freehold means you own the building and the land it stands on with no time limit. Leasehold means you own the right to occupy the property for a set number of years under a lease, with a landlord who owns the freehold. Leasehold property usually comes with ground rent, service charges and extra checks during conveyancing.
What is HM Land Registry?

HM Land Registry keeps the official record of who owns most land and property in England and Wales. After a purchase, remortgage or transfer, your conveyancer applies to update the register. Some older properties are still unregistered, and the first sale or mortgage usually triggers an application for first registration, which takes more work.
What are searches?

Searches are enquiries made to the local authority, water companies and other bodies to find out about things that affect a property but may not be obvious from viewing it. They can reveal planning history, road adoption, drainage, flood risk, environmental issues and mining in some areas. Lenders usually require them when you buy with a mortgage.
When does a sale or purchase become legally binding?

In England and Wales, a sale or purchase only becomes binding when contracts are exchanged. Before that, either side can withdraw without penalty, even late in the process. Once contracts are exchanged, pulling out usually means losing the deposit or facing a claim for losses, so the timing of exchange matters a great deal.
What is the difference between a survey and a valuation?

A mortgage valuation is carried out for the lender to check the property is worth enough to lend against. It is not a detailed inspection and may not tell you about defects. A survey is commissioned by the buyer and looks at the condition of the property in more depth. Your conveyancer deals with the legal side and does not inspect the building, so many buyers arrange a survey as well.
What is a chain?

A chain is a series of linked sales and purchases that depend on each other. If you are selling to someone who is also selling, and you are buying from someone who is buying elsewhere, you are in a chain. Everyone in it usually needs to exchange contracts and complete on the same day, so a delay anywhere can affect everyone else.
Choosing a firm
Should I use the firm my estate agent recommends?

You are free to choose any firm. Agents sometimes receive a referral fee for recommending a conveyancer, and they should tell you if they do. A recommended firm may be perfectly good, but it is sensible to compare what is on offer and to choose a firm you are comfortable with.
What is the Conveyancing Quality Scheme?

It is an accreditation run by the Law Society for solicitors' firms that meet certain standards in residential conveyancing. Many lenders require their panel firms to hold it. It is one useful sign of a firm's standards, but it is not the only one, and licensed conveyancers have their own regulatory framework.
Does it matter if the firm is local?

Much conveyancing is now done remotely, so a firm does not need to be near the property. A local firm may know common local issues, such as mining areas or flood zones. An online firm may offer longer opening hours and case tracking. Responsiveness and experience usually matter more than distance.
Can I change firms partway through?

Yes, you can move your file to another firm, but there may be charges for work already done, and the change can add delay while the new firm catches up. If you are unhappy, it is usually worth raising your concerns with the firm first and using its complaints process.
What if I am unhappy with my conveyancer?

Every regulated firm must have a complaints process and tell you about it at the start. If the firm does not resolve your complaint, you can usually take it to the Legal Ombudsman. Concerns about professional conduct can go to the Solicitors Regulation Authority or the Council for Licensed Conveyancers.
Will the same person deal with my file throughout?

It depends on the firm. Some assign a named conveyancer who handles the file from start to finish, while others use a team approach with several people involved. Ask how the firm works and how you can get updates, as this often matters more to clients than they expect.
How do I protect myself from email fraud?

Criminals sometimes target property transactions by sending fake emails that appear to come from a conveyancer, asking for money to be sent to a different account. Reputable firms warn clients about this at the start and will not change their bank details by email. Before sending any money, call your firm on a number you already know and confirm the account details.
Costs
How much does conveyancing cost?

It depends on the type of transaction, the price of the property, whether it is freehold or leasehold and any complications. Most firms give a written quote showing the legal fee, VAT and disbursements. The firm we introduce you to will give you a quote based on your own transaction before any work starts.
Why are leasehold quotes higher?

Leasehold work involves extra steps, such as reviewing the lease, obtaining a management pack from the landlord or managing agent and dealing with notices after completion. These take time and often involve fees charged by third parties, which appear as disbursements on your quote.
Do I pay if my purchase falls through?

Some firms offer a no sale, no fee or reduced fee arrangement, while others charge for work done up to that point. Disbursements already paid, such as searches, usually cannot be refunded. Ask the firm what its terms are before you instruct it.
When do I pay the conveyancer?

Many firms ask for money on account at the start to cover searches and other early disbursements. The balance of the fee is usually paid just before completion, often deducted from the sale proceeds if you are selling. Your firm will send a completion statement showing exactly what is due.
Does Leaflegal charge anything?

No. Leaflegal is free for you to use. The firm we introduce you to pays us a fee for the introduction, and that fee never changes what the firm charges you. You only pay the firm if you decide to instruct it, and the firm will set out its charges in writing before any work starts.
Is Stamp Duty included in the quote?

Stamp Duty Land Tax in England or Land Transaction Tax in Wales is a tax, not a legal fee. Many quotes show an estimate so you can plan, but the final amount depends on your circumstances and the rules at the time. Your conveyancer will usually calculate it, submit the return and pay it from funds you provide.
Timescales
How long does conveyancing take?

It varies widely. A remortgage might take a few weeks, while a purchase in a chain can take several months. The length of the chain, search returns, mortgage offers, leasehold information and how quickly everyone responds all play a part. Your conveyancer can give a better estimate once they have seen the paperwork.
Can I speed things up?

You cannot control everyone in the chain, but you can make sure you are not the hold up. Instruct a firm early, send ID and documents promptly, return forms quickly and keep your mortgage broker and estate agent in the loop. Sellers can help by preparing their paperwork before a buyer is found.
Why is my transaction taking so long?

Common causes include waiting for searches, a slow mortgage offer, a leasehold management pack that has not arrived, unanswered enquiries or problems further along the chain. Your conveyancer should be able to tell you what is outstanding and who it is waiting on.
How long between exchange and completion?

It is agreed between buyers and sellers and can be anything from the same day to several weeks. Many people choose a gap of a week or two to arrange removals. In a chain, everyone needs to agree on the same completion date.
What happens on completion day?

On completion day, the buyer's money is sent to the seller's conveyancer, usually through the banking system in the morning or around midday, depending on the chain. Once the seller's conveyancer confirms the money has arrived, the estate agent is told to release the keys. In a chain, money often has to pass from the bottom of the chain upwards, so timing can vary.
Using Leaflegal
What does Leaflegal do?

Leaflegal is a free introduction service. You fill in a short form about your property matter and we introduce you to one regulated firm that handles that kind of work. The firm then contacts you to talk through your situation and give you a quote.
Is Leaflegal a law firm?

No. Leaflegal is not a law firm and does not give legal advice. Any advice about your transaction comes from the firm you are introduced to, which is regulated and carries its own professional insurance. Our role is simply to match your enquiry with one firm that handles your kind of property matter.
Do I have to instruct the firm?

No. There is no obligation. You can speak to the firm, ask questions about how it works, get a quote and then decide whether to go ahead. If you choose not to, you do not need to give a reason, and there is no charge for the conversation or the quote.
How quickly will the firm contact me?

Firms usually get in touch within one working day of your enquiry, and often sooner. If you have an urgent deadline, such as a remortgage deal ending or a developer's exchange date, mention it on the form so the firm knows.
What information will the firm need from me?

To begin with, the firm will usually want to know the property address, the agreed price, whether it is freehold or leasehold, whether you have a mortgage and roughly when you hope to move. If you decide to instruct the firm, it will then ask for identity documents, proof of address and details of where your money is coming from.
